title: What Regulatory Structures Would Ensure AI Ecosystem Diversity? Backcasting from Systemic Risk Standards

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: identifying gaps in regulatory proposals is valuable but the connection between the analysis and actual regulatory change has significant intermediary steps.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: requires understanding of regulatory frameworks (EU AI Act, US exec orders) and financial regulation analogies. CS students would need guidance on policy analysis methods.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Open-ended: comparing regulatory frameworks across domains and identifying minimum requirements is a broad policy review without clear deliverable boundaries.

novelty.reasoning: The EU AI Act (entered force August 2024, GPAI rules effective August 2025) addresses systemic risk from general-purpose AI models but does not include explicit ecosystem diversity requirements. The ESRB Advisory Scientific Committee report (December 2025) discusses AI-driven systemic risk in financial markets and model uniformity. The Oxford Law Blog (2025) directly addresses AI regulatory capture and fragmentation. An AI & Society paper (2025) argues that captured AI-safety regulations create harms. The FLI AI Safety Index calls for quantitative thresholds. However, the specific backcasting exercise of identifying minimum regulatory structures needed to ensure AI ecosystem diversity, drawing analogies from financial systemic risk standards, has not been systematically conducted. The framing adds value but builds heavily on existing policy analysis.

evidence: ESRB Advisory Scientific Committee Report: AI and Systemic Risk. December 2025.
AI Safety and Regulatory Capture. AI & Society, Springer, 2025.
AI Regulation: The Politics of Fragmentation and Regulatory Capture. Oxford Law Blogs, 2025.
